reason: εἰς τέλος is rendered 'to the end' throughout these Psalms (73:1, 3, 10, 11, 19; 78:5); 'completely' interprets.

old: Do justice for the orphan and the poor; vindicate the lowly and the needy.
new: Do justice for the orphan and the poor; justify the lowly and the needy.
reason: δικαιώσατε is δικαιόω, rendered "justify" throughout this edition.

old: A prayer of David. Incline Your ear, Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy.
new: A prayer for David. Incline Your ear, Lord, and hear me, for I am poor and needy.
reason: τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; the edition renders the superscription dative as "for" ("for Asaph," "for the sons of Korah," "for David" in 90:1, 93:1, 94:1).

old: "Mother Zion," a man will say, and a Man was born in her, and He Himself, the Most High, founded her.
new: "Mother Zion," a man will say, and "A man was born in her," and "He Himself, the Most High, founded her."
reason: The capitals on Ἄνθρωπος and Αὐτός follow this text's convention of capitalizing the first word of quoted speech (cf. 81:6, 82:5, 93:7), not a title; capital "Man" imposes a messianic referent the Greek does not mark.

old: Whereas the Hebrew reads "Of Zion it shall be said, 'This one and that one was born in her,'" the Greek reads "'Mother Zion,' a man will say, and a Man was born in her." The capitalization of "Man" and "He Himself" preserves the Saints Greek Critical Text, reflecting the ancient Messianic reading of the verse.
new: Whereas the Hebrew reads "Of Zion it shall be said, 'This one and that one was born in her,'" the Greek reads "'Mother Zion,' a man will say." In this Greek text the capitals on Anthropos and Autos mark the start of quoted words, as elsewhere in the Psalms (e.g., 81:6).
reason: The note's claim that the Greek capitals reflect a messianic reading is false for this text (capitals mark speech openings) and is a doctrinal comment.

old: The Septuagint superscription assigns this psalm to Wednesday ("the fourth day of the week"), and ἐκδικήσεων is plural ("acts of vengeance"). Greek ἐπαρρησιάσατο ("acted boldly" or "spoke openly") is an aorist indicative rather than the Hebrew imperative "shine forth."
new: The Septuagint superscription assigns this psalm to Wednesday ("the fourth day of the week"), and ἐκδικήσεων is plural ("acts of vengeance"). Greek ἐπαρρησιάσατο ("acted boldly" or "spoke openly") is an aorist indicative, where the Hebrew is usually rendered as an imperative ("shine forth").
reason: The Masoretic form הוֹפִיעַ is pointed as a perfect and only usually translated as an imperative; the note overstated the Hebrew.

old: When the house is being built after the captivity; a song of David. Sing a new song to the Lord; sing to the Lord, all the earth.
new: When the house is being built after the captivity; a song for David. Sing a new song to the Lord; sing to the Lord, all the earth.
reason: ᾠδὴ τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 90:1, 93:1, 94:1.

old: Of David, when his land is being established. The Lord has become king; the earth will exult; let many islands be glad.
new: For David, when his land is being established. The Lord has become king; the earth will exult; let many islands be glad.
reason: Τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 90:1, 93:1, 94:1.

old: The Greek superscription ("Of David, when his land is being established") has no counterpart in Hebrew Psalm 97. Here and in 95:10, the aorist ἐβασίλευσεν carries an ingressive sense ("has become king").
new: The Greek superscription ("For David, when his land is being established") has no counterpart in Hebrew Psalm 97. Here and in 95:10, the aorist ἐβασίλευσεν carries an ingressive sense ("has become king").
reason: Note quotation updated to match the corrected superscription.

old: A psalm of David. Sing a new song to the Lord, for the Lord has done wondrous things; His right hand and His holy arm have brought Him salvation.
new: A psalm for David. Sing a new song to the Lord, for the Lord has done wondrous things; His right hand and His holy arm have brought Him salvation.
reason: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 93:1 (identical Greek).

old: The Greek superscription adds "of David" (τῷ Δαυίδ), whereas Hebrew Psalm 98 reads only "A psalm." The dative αὐτῷ ("Him") indicates that His right hand and holy arm achieved salvation on His behalf.
new: The Greek superscription adds "for David" (τῷ Δαυίδ), whereas Hebrew Psalm 98 reads only "A psalm." The dative αὐτῷ ("Him") indicates that His right hand and holy arm achieved salvation on His behalf.
reason: Note quotation updated to match the corrected superscription.

old: A psalm of David. The Lord has become king; let peoples be angry. He who sits upon the cherubim—let the earth be shaken.
new: A psalm for David. The Lord has become king; let peoples be angry. He who sits upon the cherubim—let the earth be shaken.
reason: Ψαλμὸς τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 93:1 (identical Greek).

old: The Septuagint includes the superscription "A psalm of David" (absent in Hebrew Ps 99) and renders the verb as "be angry" (ὀργιζέσθωσαν) rather than "tremble." The aorist ἐβασίλευσεν is ingressive ("has become king" or "reigned").
new: The Septuagint includes the superscription "A psalm for David" (absent in Hebrew Ps 99) and renders the verb as "be angry" (ὀργιζέσθωσαν) rather than "tremble." The aorist ἐβασίλευσεν is ingressive ("has become king" or "reigned").
reason: Note quotation updated to match the corrected superscription.

old: A psalm of David. Mercy and justice I will sing to You, Lord;
new: A psalm for David. Mercy and justice I will sing to You, Lord;
reason: Τῷ Δαυὶδ ψαλμός is dative; rendered "for David" as in 93:1.

old: The sons of Your servants will settle, and their offspring will be guided straight forever."
new: The sons of Your servants will settle, and their seed will be guided straight forever."
reason: σπέρμα is rendered "seed" in this edition's OT (cf. 88:5, 88:30, 88:37).

old: Of David. Bless the Lord, my soul, and everything within me, His holy name.
new: For David. Bless the Lord, my soul, and everything within me, His holy name.
reason: Τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 90:1, 93:1, 94:1.

old: Of David. Bless the Lord, my soul. Lord, Lord, my God, how exceedingly You have been magnified! You clothed Yourself with thanksgiving and splendor,
new: For David. Bless the Lord, my soul. Lord, Lord, my God, how exceedingly You have been magnified! You clothed Yourself with thanksgiving and splendor,
reason: Τῷ Δαυίδ is dative; rendered "for David" as in 90:1, 93:1, 94:1.

old: wrapping Yourself in light like a garment, stretching out heaven like a curtain;
new: wrapping Yourself in light like a garment, stretching out heaven like a skin;
reason: δέρρις means a skin or hide (leather covering); "curtain" follows the Hebrew יְרִיעָה.

old: offspring of Abraham, His servants, sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.
new: seed of Abraham, His servants, sons of Jacob, His chosen ones.
reason: σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ: σπέρμα is rendered "seed" in this edition's OT.

old: and He established it for Jacob as a decree, and for Israel an everlasting covenant,
new: and He established it for Jacob as a decree, and for Israel an eternal covenant,
reason: διαθήκην αἰώνιον: αἰώνιος is rendered "eternal" in this edition (cf. 77:66).

old: He placed in them the words of His signs and wonders in the land of Ham.
new: He placed for them the words of His signs and wonders in the land of Ham.
reason: This Greek has the bare dative αὐτοῖς (no ἐν); "in them" follows editions reading ἐν αὐτοῖς.

old: and to cast down their offspring among the nations and to scatter them in the lands.
new: and to cast down their seed among the nations and to scatter them in the lands.
reason: τὸ σπέρμα αὐτῶν: the edition's OT convention renders σπέρμα (descendants) as the literal collective "seed".

old: For the end; a psalm of David. God, do not pass over my praise in silence,
new: For the end; a psalm for David. God, do not pass over my praise in silence,
reason: Psalm heading τῷ Δαυίδ → "for David" (Psalter-wide)

old: A psalm of David. The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at My right hand until I set Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet."
new: A psalm for David. The Lord said to my Lord, "Sit at My right hand until I set Your enemies as a footstool for Your feet."
reason: Psalm heading τῷ Δαυίδ → "for David" (Psalter-wide)

old: The Septuagint differs markedly from the Hebrew here, reading "with You is dominion [Greek arche, also 'beginning'] ... from the womb before the morning star I brought You forth," a prominent Christological passage in early Christian tradition.
new: The Septuagint differs markedly from the Hebrew here, reading "with You is dominion [Greek arche, also 'beginning'] ... from the womb before the morning star I brought You forth."
reason: The closing clause is reception-history/doctrinal comment rather than an explanation of the Greek; the factual textual comparison is kept.

old: His offspring will be powerful on the earth; the generation of the upright will be blessed.
new: His seed will be powerful on the earth; the generation of the upright will be blessed.
reason: τὸ σπέρμα αὐτοῦ: the edition's OT convention renders σπέρμα (descendants) as the literal collective "seed".

old: And I will keep Your law continually, forever and to the age of the age.
new: And I will keep Your law continually, forever, and forever and ever.
reason: Psalter-wide formula

old: I have inclined my heart to do Your statutes forever, for the recompense of all.
new: I have inclined my heart to do Your statutes forever, continually, as a recompense.
reason: διὰ παντός is the fixed idiom "continually" (so rendered throughout this psalm), and the accusative ἄμειψιν ("recompense") cannot be "the recompense of all"; παντός is governed by διά, not by ἄμειψιν.

old: Greek uses the passive of rhyomai ("was rescued ... were rescued"), emphasizing divine deliverance rather than an active escape, and pairs "hunters" (thēreuontōn) with "prey" (thēran) in v. 6.
new: Greek uses the passive of rhyomai ("was rescued ... were rescued") where the Hebrew reads "escaped," and pairs "hunters" (thēreuontōn) with "prey" (thēran) in v. 6.
reason: "Emphasizing divine deliverance" is theological interpretation; the note now states only the neutral lexical/textual fact.

old: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("servants of the LORD"), the Greek places "the Lord" in the accusative as the direct object of "praise" and leaves "servants" as a vocative.
new: Unlike the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("servants of the Lord"), the Greek places "the Lord" in the accusative as the direct object of "praise" and leaves "servants" as a vocative.
reason: House style forbids capitalized LORD; κύριος is rendered "the Lord" throughout.

old: The Greek begins with a finite verb, ἐμακάρισαν ("They called blessed"), contrasting popular admiration of material prosperity with the psalmist's declaration that the people whose God is the Lord are truly blessed.
new: The Greek begins with a finite verb, ἐμακάρισαν ("They called blessed"), where the Hebrew reads "Blessed is the people."
reason: The second half of the note was interpretive commentary (adding "truly") rather than an explanation of the Greek.

old: Let all Your works give thanks to You, Lord, and let Your holy ones bless You.
new: Let all Your works give thanks to You, Lord, and let Your devout ones bless You.
reason: οἱ ὅσιοί σου is "Your devout ones" elsewhere in this section (131:9, 131:16, 149:5, 149:9); "holy ones" is the rendering of ἅγιοι.

old: The Greek uses the plural "Your hands" and places εὐδοκίας ("goodwill" or "favor") in the genitive, expressing that God fills every living creature with His goodwill rather than satisfying their desire as in the Masoretic Text.
new: The Greek uses the plural "Your hands" where the Masoretic Text has the singular, and the genitive εὐδοκίας ("goodwill," "favor," or "good pleasure") expresses what every living creature is filled with.
reason: εὐδοκίας does not specify whose goodwill it is (it is the usual equivalent of the Hebrew word for favor/desire), so the claimed contrast with the Hebrew interprets the Greek.

old: For the Lord takes pleasure in His people, and He will exalt the humble with salvation.
new: For the Lord takes pleasure in His people, and He will exalt the meek with salvation.
reason: πρᾳεῖς is "the meek" in 146:6 (cf. πραΰτης "meekness" 131:1); "humble" is used for ταπεινός.

old: Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and flute.
new: Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and a musical instrument.
reason: ὀργάνῳ is the general word "instrument" (rendered "musical instrument" in 136:2 and 151:2); "flute" follows the Hebrew.

old: Greek organon literally means 'musical instrument' and is used in the Septuagint (here and in 151:2) for a wind instrument such as a flute or pipe.
new: Greek organon is a general word for a musical instrument (as in 136:2 and 151:2); the Hebrew here names a pipe or flute.
reason: Note claimed ὄργανον means a wind instrument here and in 151:2, which the Greek does not specify and which the edition's own 151:2 does not follow.

old: for you will receive a wreath of graces on your head, and a golden collar around your neck.
new: for you will receive a crown of graces on your head, and a golden collar around your neck.
reason: The same phrase στέφανον χαρίτων is "a crown of graces" in 4:9.

old: Verse 1:16 is absent in the Septuagint tradition, which proceeds directly from 1:15 to 1:17 and reads ἀδίκως ("unjustly") rather than "in vain."
new: Verse 1:16 is absent from this Greek text, which proceeds directly from 1:15 to 1:17; the Greek reads ἀδίκως ("unjustly") where the Hebrew reads "in vain."
reason: The claim that 1:16 is absent from the whole Septuagint tradition overstates; the note should describe the Greek text in hand.

old: Do, son, what I command you, and save yourself; for you have come into the hands of evil men because of your friend. Go without growing faint, and also spur on your friend for whom you became guarantor.
new: Do, son, what I command you, and save yourself; for you have come into the hands of evil men because of your friend. Do not grow faint, and also spur on your friend for whom you became guarantor.
reason: ἴσθι μὴ ἐκλυόμενος is the imperative of "be" with a participle ("be not growing faint", cf. ἴσθι πεποιθώς "Be trusting" 3:5); "Go" follows the Hebrew "go".

old: Here and in 6:6, the Greek form isthi represents a manuscript spelling of ithi ('Go!'), rather than the imperative of 'be' (compare 5:20).
new: Greek isthi here is the imperative of 'be' with a participle (literally 'be not growing faint'); in 6:6 the same form stands for ithi ('Go').
reason: With a participle, ἴσθι in 6:3 is the normal periphrastic imperative of εἰμί; only in 6:6 (followed by πρὸς τὸν μύρμηκα) does it require "Go".

old: the eye of an insolent man, an unjust tongue, hands shedding the blood of a just man,
new: the eye of an insolent man, an unjust tongue, hands shedding the blood of a righteous man,
reason: δίκαιος of a person is "righteous" in this book (e.g. ἄνδρα δίκαιον "a righteous man" 1:11).

old: Good understanding gives favor, and to know law belongs to a good mind, but the ways of those who despise are in ruin.
new: Good understanding gives favor, and to know the law belongs to a good mind, but the ways of those who despise are in ruin.
reason: τὸ δὲ γνῶναι νόμον is identical to 9:10 (τὸ γὰρ γνῶναι νόμον), which the edition renders "to know the law"; align the identical clause.

old: Insight is a fountain of life to those who possess it, but the discipline of fools is evil.
new: Insight is a spring of life to those who possess it, but the discipline of fools is evil.
reason: πηγὴ ζωῆς is rendered "spring of life" in 10:11, 13:14 and 14:27; same phrase, same sense.

old: A word in a man's heart is deep water, and a river springs up, and a fountain of life.
new: A word in a man's heart is deep water, and a river springs up, and a spring of life.
reason: πηγὴ ζωῆς is rendered "spring of life" in 10:11, 13:14 and 14:27; same phrase, same sense.

old: Luxury is not fitting for a fool, nor if a household servant begins to rule with insolence.
new: Luxury is not beneficial for a fool, nor if a household servant begins to rule with insolence.
reason: οὐ συμφέρει means "is not beneficial/advantageous"; "is not fitting" reflects the Hebrew (na'weh) rather than the Greek.

old: When an undisciplined person is punished, the evil person becomes more shrewd, and when a wise person understands, he will receive knowledge.
new: When an unrestrained person is punished, the evil person becomes more shrewd, and when a wise person understands, he will receive knowledge.
reason: ἀκόλαστος is "unrestrained" in 19:29 and 20:1; "undisciplined" is the edition's rendering of ἀπαίδευτος (15:12, 17:21).

old: The Septuagint reads "courage" and "for the ungodly," diverging notably from the Masoretic Text ("understanding" and "against the LORD").
new: The Septuagint reads "courage" and "for the ungodly," diverging notably from the Masoretic Text ("understanding" and "against the Lord").
reason: House style never uses capitalized LORD; the divine name is "the Lord" in notes as in verses.

old: The Greek reads οὐδαμοῦ πεσεῖται ("it will fall nowhere," where some manuscripts read φανεῖται, "will appear") and refers to τοῦ προεστηκότος αὐτοῦ ("the one set over him"), which may denote a patron or master, or metaphorically God.
new: The Greek reads οὐδαμοῦ πεσεῖται ("it will fall nowhere," where some manuscripts read φανεῖται, "will appear") and refers to τοῦ προεστηκότος αὐτοῦ ("the one set over him"), which may denote a patron or master.
reason: "or metaphorically God" is speculative interpretation of the referent, not an explanation of the Greek; keep the note to lexis and textual reading.

old: The second sentence ('There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace') is a Septuagint addition shared verbatim with Sirach 4:21.
new: The second sentence ('There is a shame that brings sin, and there is a shame that is glory and grace') is a Septuagint addition nearly identical to Sirach 4:21.
reason: Sirach 4:21 reads ἔστιν γὰρ αἰσχύνη..., adding γάρ, so the wording is not strictly verbatim.

old: "The Assembler" translates Greek Ekklesiastes ("one who convenes or addresses an assembly"), traditionally transliterated "Ecclesiastes" or rendered "the Preacher."
new: "The Assembler" translates Greek Ekklesiastes ("one who convenes or addresses an assembly").
reason: Notes should explain the Greek, not report how other translations render the title.

old: I acquired male slaves and female slaves, and homeborn ones became mine; and also a great possession of herd and flock became mine, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem;
new: I acquired male servants and female servants, and homeborn ones became mine; and also a great possession of herd and flock became mine, beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem;
reason: OT convention renders δοῦλος as "servant" (as in 5:11 and 7:21 of this book); παιδίσκας pairs with it as "female servants."

old: Greek renders the obscure Hebrew phrase shiddah weshiddot as "a male cupbearer and female cupbearers" (oinochoon kai oinochoas, often rendered "concubines" from the Hebrew).
new: Greek renders the obscure Hebrew phrase shiddah weshiddot as "a male cupbearer and female cupbearers" (oinochoon kai oinochoas).
reason: Removes a claim about how other translations render the Hebrew; the note should explain the Greek.

old: because there is a man whose toil is in wisdom and in knowledge and in courage, and to a man who did not toil in it he will give his portion; this too is futility and a great evil.
new: because there is a man whose toil is in wisdom and in knowledge and in prowess, and to a man who did not toil in it he will give his portion; this too is futility and a great evil.
reason: ἀνδρεία is rendered "prowess" in 4:4 and 5:10 (skill/capability, per the 4:4 note); "courage" gives a different sense here.

old: Greek reads a declarative statement ("For it happens to man...") rather than the Hebrew rhetorical question ("For what does a man have...?"). In v. 24, Greek (like the unemended Hebrew) lacks "except/better," implying that enjoying toil is not a good man produces himself but comes from God (cf. v. 25, where Greek reads "drink apart from Him" vs. MT "have enjoyment apart from me").
new: Greek reads a declarative statement ("For it happens to man...") rather than the Hebrew rhetorical question ("For what does a man have...?"). In v. 24, Greek (like the unemended Hebrew) lacks "except/better"; in v. 25 Greek reads "drink apart from Him" vs. MT "have enjoyment apart from me."
reason: Drops the interpretive inference ("implying that...") and keeps the factual textual observations.

old: If you see oppression of a poor person and robbery of justice and righteousness in a province, do not be amazed at the matter; a high one is over a high one to watch, and high ones are over them;
new: If you see oppression of a poor person and robbery of justice and righteousness in a region, do not be amazed at the matter; a high one is over a high one to watch, and high ones are over them;
reason: χώρα is "land/region" and is rendered "regions" in 2:8; "province" reflects the Hebrew medinah rather than the Greek.

old: For extortion drives a wise man mad and destroys the heart of his nobility.
new: For oppression drives a wise man mad and destroys the heart of his nobility.
reason: συκοφαντία is rendered "oppression" elsewhere in this book (4:1; 5:7).

old: for very often he will treat you wickedly and in many ways he will afflict your heart, because in the same way you also cursed others.
new: for very often he will treat you wickedly and many times he will afflict your heart, because in the same way you also cursed others.
reason: καθόδους πολλάς means "many times/occasions" (κάθοδος = recurrence), not "in many ways."

old: When I gave my heart to know wisdom and to see the busyness that has been done on the earth, for both by day and by night one does not see sleep with his eyes,
new: When I gave my heart to know wisdom and to see the preoccupation that has been done on the earth, for both by day and by night one does not see sleep with his eyes,
reason: περισπασμός is rendered "preoccupation" throughout the book (1:13; 2:23, 26; 3:10; 4:8; 5:13).

old: futility in all things. There is one event for the righteous and for the ungodly, for the good and for the bad, and for the clean and for the unclean, and for the one who sacrifices and for the one who does not sacrifice. As is the good man, so is the sinner; so is the one who swears, just as the one who fears the oath.
new: futility in all things. There is one fate for the righteous and for the ungodly, for the good and for the bad, and for the clean and for the unclean, and for the one who sacrifices and for the one who does not sacrifice. As is the good man, so is the sinner; so is the one who swears, just as the one who fears the oath.
reason: συνάντημα ἕν is rendered "one fate" in 2:14-15 and 3:19.

old: This is an evil in everything done under the sun, that there is one event for all. And also the heart of the sons of man is filled with evil, and madness is in their heart during their life, and after them, to the dead.
new: This is an evil in everything done under the sun, that there is one fate for all. And also the heart of the sons of man is filled with evil, and madness is in their heart during their life, and after them, to the dead.
reason: συνάντημα ἕν is rendered "one fate" in 2:14-15 and 3:19.

old: I turned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, and war is not to the mighty, nor bread to the wise man, nor wealth to the discerning, nor favor to those who know; for time and chance will meet all of them.
new: I turned and saw under the sun that the race is not to the swift, and war is not to the mighty, and also bread is not to the wise man, nor wealth to the discerning, and also favor is not to those who know; for time and chance will meet all of them.
reason: The twice-repeated καί γε ("and also") is left unrepresented; the edition renders καί γε elsewhere in the context (9:12, 9:13, 10:3).

old: I saw slaves on horses, and princes walking like slaves on the ground.
new: I saw servants on horses, and princes walking like servants on the ground.
reason: δούλους is rendered "servant(s)" by the OT convention of this edition (cf. 5:11, 7:21 in this book).

old: Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you rest at noon, so that I never become like one veiled beside the herds of your comrades.
new: Tell me, you whom my soul has loved, where you pasture, where you rest at noon, so that I do not become like one veiled beside the herds of your comrades.
reason: μή ποτε is "lest/so that ... not"; "never" adds an absolute intensifier.

old: Look, you are handsome, my kinsman, and indeed lovely; moreover, our couch is shaded;
new: Look, you are handsome, my kinsman, and indeed lovely; by our couch, shady;
reason: πρὸς κλίνῃ ἡμῶν σύσκιος is "by our couch, shady" (πρός + dative; nominative σύσκιος cannot modify dative κλίνῃ); "moreover, our couch is shaded" follows the Hebrew.

old: Catch for us little foxes that ruin vineyards, and our vineyards are in blossom.
new: Catch for us little foxes that ruin vineyards, and our vines are in blossom.
reason: αἱ ἄμπελοι ἡμῶν κυπρίζουσαι is "our vines" (ἄμπελος), distinct from ἀμπελῶνας "vineyards"; cf. 2:13 "the vines are in blossom."

old: He made its pillars of silver, and its backrest golden; its seat is purple, its interior is inlaid with stone, love from the daughters of Jerusalem.
new: He made its pillars of silver, and its backrest golden; its step is purple, its interior is inlaid with stone, love from the daughters of Jerusalem.
reason: ἐπίβασις means a step or means of mounting (cf. Ps 103:3 "ascent"); "seat" reflects the Hebrew merkab.

old: Let my beloved come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his choice trees. I have entered into a garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices, I have eaten my bread with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, companions, and drink and become drunk, brothers.
new: Let my kinsman come down into his garden and eat the fruit of his choice trees. I have entered into a garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spices, I have eaten my bread with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk. Eat, companions, and drink and become drunk, brothers.
reason: ἀδελφιδός is rendered "kinsman" in 1:13-2:17 and 7:10-8:14 (see note at 1:13); chapters 5-6 and 8:5 switch to "beloved" for the same word.

old: Greek adelphidos (literally "nephew" or "dear kinsman") serves throughout Septuagint Song of Songs as a term of endearment ("beloved"). The Greek text here also reads "into a garden" (without "my"), "my bread" (where the Hebrew has "my honeycomb"), and "brothers" (where the Hebrew has "beloved/lovers").
new: The Greek text here reads "into a garden" (without "my"), "my bread" (where the Hebrew has "my honeycomb"), and "brothers" (where the Hebrew has "beloved/lovers").
reason: The first sentence justified "beloved" for ἀδελφιδός, which is now rendered "kinsman" consistently as explained at 1:13.

old: I am sleeping, and my heart is awake. The voice of my beloved! He is knocking at the door: "Open to me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my perfect one, for my head has been filled with dew and my locks with the drops of the night."
new: I am sleeping, and my heart is awake. The voice of my kinsman! He is knocking at the door: "Open to me, my sister, my companion, my dove, my perfect one, for my head has been filled with dew and my locks with the drops of the night."
reason: ἀδελφιδοῦ μου: same term rendered "my kinsman" in 2:8 (identical φωνὴ ἀδελφιδοῦ μου).

old: My beloved sent his hand from the opening, and my belly was stirred for him.
new: My kinsman sent his hand from the opening, and my belly was stirred for him.
reason: ἀδελφιδός μου is rendered "my kinsman" elsewhere in the book (1:13, 2:3, 7:11).

old: I rose to open to my beloved; my hands dripped myrrh, my fingers full myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
new: I rose to open to my kinsman; my hands dripped myrrh, my fingers full myrrh, on the handles of the bolt.
reason: τῷ ἀδελφιδῷ μου: "my kinsman" as in 7:10-11.

old: I opened to my beloved; my beloved had passed by; my soul went out at his word; I sought him and did not find him, I called him and he did not answer me.
new: I opened to my kinsman; my kinsman had passed by; my soul went out at his word; I sought him and did not find him, I called him and he did not answer me.
reason: ἀδελφιδῷ μου / ἀδελφιδός μου: "my kinsman" as elsewhere in the book.

old: I have put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field: if you find my beloved, what should you report to him? That I am wounded with love.
new: I have put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field: if you find my kinsman, what should you report to him? That I am wounded with love.
reason: τὸν ἀδελφιδόν μου: "my kinsman" as elsewhere in the book.

old: What is your beloved more than another beloved, beautiful one among women, what is your beloved more than another beloved, that you have put us under oath like this?
new: What is your kinsman more than another kinsman, beautiful one among women, what is your kinsman more than another kinsman, that you have put us under oath like this?
reason: ἀδελφιδός σου ἀπὸ ἀδελφιδοῦ: same term rendered "kinsman" elsewhere in the book.

old: My beloved is white and ruddy, selected out from ten thousands.
new: My kinsman is white and ruddy, selected out from ten thousands.
reason: Ἀδελφιδός μου: "my kinsman" as in 2:9 (ὅμοιός ἐστιν ἀδελφιδός μου).

old: His throat is sweetnesses, and he is wholly desire. This is my beloved, and this is my companion, daughters of Jerusalem.
new: His throat is sweetnesses, and he is wholly desire. This is my kinsman, and this is my companion, daughters of Jerusalem.
reason: οὗτος ἀδελφιδός μου: "my kinsman" as elsewhere in the book.

old: Where has your beloved gone, beautiful one among women? Where has your beloved looked? And we will seek him with you.
new: Where has your kinsman gone, beautiful one among women? Where has your kinsman looked? And we will seek him with you.
reason: ὁ ἀδελφιδός σου (twice): "kinsman" as elsewhere in the book.

old: Here the Greek text reads Adelphos mou ("My brother") rather than adelphidos mou ("my beloved"), which appears in 6:1 and 6:3.
new: Here the Greek text reads Adelphos mou ("My brother") rather than adelphidos ("kinsman"), which appears in 6:1 and 6:3.
reason: Aligns the note with the standardized rendering "kinsman"; 6:1 has adelphidos sou, not adelphidos mou.

old: I belong to my beloved, and my beloved belongs to me, the one who shepherds among the lilies.
new: I belong to my kinsman, and my kinsman belongs to me, the one who shepherds among the lilies.
reason: τῷ ἀδελφιδῷ μου καὶ ἀδελφιδός μου: "my kinsman" as in the parallel 7:11 ("I belong to my kinsman").

old: I have put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you do not rouse or awaken love until it wishes.
new: I have put you under oath, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and by the strengths of the field, that you do not rouse and awaken love until it wishes.
reason: ἐγείρητε καὶ ἐξεγείρητε has καί, rendered "rouse and awaken" in the identical refrains 2:7 and 3:5.

old: Who is this coming up made white, leaning on her beloved? Under an apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor with you.
new: Who is this coming up made white, leaning on her kinsman? Under an apple tree I awakened you; there your mother was in labor with you; there she who bore you was in labor with you.
reason: ἐπὶ τὸν ἀδελφιδὸν αὐτῆς: "kinsman" as elsewhere in the book.

old: Flee, my kinsman, and be like a gazelle or a fawn of the deer upon the mountains of spices.
new: Flee, my kinsman, and be like a gazelle or a fawn of the stags upon the mountains of spices.
reason: νεβρῷ (τῶν) ἐλάφων is "fawn of stags" in 2:9 and 2:17.

old: Pe. Zion spread out her hands; there is no one who comforts her. The Lord gave a command concerning Jacob: all around him are those who afflict him; Jerusalem has become a menstruating woman in their midst.
new: Pe. Zion spread out her hands; there is no one who comforts her. The Lord gave a command to Jacob: all around him are those who afflict him; Jerusalem has become a menstruating woman in their midst.
reason: ἐνετείλατο ... τῷ Ἰακώβ is a plain dative of the person commanded; "concerning" reflects the Hebrew preposition.

old: Beth. In the day of His anger the Lord engulfed without sparing all the beautiful things of Jacob; He tore down in His fury the strongholds of the daughter of Judah; He pressed to the ground and profaned her kings and her rulers.
new: Beth. In the day of His anger the Lord engulfed, not sparing; all the beautiful things of Jacob He tore down in His fury; the strongholds of the daughter of Judah He pressed to the ground; He profaned her kings and her rulers.
reason: In this Greek, πάντα τὰ ὡραῖα Ἰακώβ is the object of καθεῖλεν, τὰ ὀχυρώματα the object of ἐκόλλησεν εἰς τὴν γῆν, and βασιλέας/ἄρχοντας the object of ἐβεβήλωσεν only; the English reassigns the objects along the Hebrew clause division.

old: Gimel. Even though I will cry out and shout, He has blocked off my prayer.
new: Gimel. And indeed I will cry out and shout; He has blocked off my prayer.
reason: Καί γε κεκράξομαι καὶ βοήσω is a coordinate statement ("and indeed I will cry out"); the concessive "even though" reflects the Hebrew gam ki, which the Greek does not reproduce.

old: Heh. He bent His bow and set me up like a target for an arrow.
new: He. He bent His bow and set me up like a target for an arrow.
reason: Ἥ is rendered "He." in 1:5, 2:5 and 4:5; "Heh" is the only divergent spelling of this acrostic letter.

old: Vav. And the iniquity of the daughter of my people became greater than the iniquities of Sodom, which was overthrown as in haste, and they did not weary their hands in her.
new: Waw. And the iniquity of the daughter of my people became greater than the iniquities of Sodom, which was overthrown as in haste, and they did not weary their hands in her.
reason: Οὐαύ is rendered "Waw." in 1:6, 2:6 and 3:15.

old: Resh. The breath of our face, the anointed Lord, was captured in their destructions, of whom we said, "In His shadow we will live among the nations."
new: Resh. The breath of our face, the anointed Lord, was captured in their destructions, of whom we said, "In his shadow we will live among the nations."
reason: The referent of χριστὸς Κύριος (an anointed one who is captured) is disputed; the capitalized "His" silently decides it as divine, while lowercase keeps the Greek's ambiguity.

old: The Greek reads nominative christos Kyrios ("the anointed Lord") rather than the Hebrew genitive "the LORD's anointed," a reading widely interpreted Christologically by early Christian writers.
new: The Greek reads nominative christos Kyrios ("the anointed Lord") rather than the Hebrew genitive "the Lord's anointed."
reason: Removes a claim about later interpretation (not about the Greek) and the capitalized LORD, which the house style excludes.

old: Tav. Your iniquity has come to an end, daughter of Zion; He will no longer carry you into exile. He has visited your iniquities, daughter of Edom; He has uncovered your ungodly deeds.
new: Taw. Your iniquity has come to an end, daughter of Zion; He will no longer carry you into exile. He has visited your iniquities, daughter of Edom; He has uncovered your ungodly deeds.
reason: Θαύ is rendered "Taw." in 1:22, 2:22 and 3:65.

old: Slaves have ruled over us; there is no redeemer from their hand.
new: Servants have ruled over us; there is no redeemer from their hand.
reason: δοῦλοι is rendered "servants" by this edition's OT convention for δοῦλος.

old: For crooked reasonings separate one from God, and His power, when tested, convicts the foolish.
new: For crooked reasonings separate one from God, and the power, when tested, convicts the foolish.
reason: ἡ δύναμις has only the article; "His" supplies a possessor and silently decides whose power is meant.

old: The verb "hastened" (espeusen) has no explicit object in Greek; it may be taken intransitively of the righteous person ("he hastened") or, as in the Latin Vulgate, with the Lord as subject ("He hastened [to remove him]").
new: The verb "hastened" (espeusen) has no explicit object in Greek; it may be taken intransitively of the righteous person ("he hastened") or with the Lord as subject ("He hastened [to remove him]").
reason: Notes should explain the Greek, not report what another translation (the Vulgate) does; the ambiguity statement stands on its own.

old: Greek reads eneplēsthēmen ("we were filled / had our fill"); some translators emend the text to eneplakēmen ("we were entangled").
new: Greek reads eneplēsthēmen ("we were filled / had our fill"); a conjectural emendation reads eneplakēmen ("we were entangled").
reason: Notes should describe the Greek and its readings, not what other translators do.

old: Following the critical Greek reading genesin ("origin" or "source"); some later witnesses and versions read genetin ("mother" or "begetter").
new: Following the critical Greek reading genesin ("origin" or "source"); other witnesses and versions read genetin ("mother" or "begetter").
reason: The characterization of the γενέτιν witnesses as "later" is not supported; state the variant neutrally.

old: Greek enkratēs appears without an explicit object and can mean either "in possession [of wisdom]" (fitting 8:18 and 9:4, 17) or "self-controlled/continent" (as rendered in the Latin Vulgate).
new: Greek enkratēs appears without an explicit object and can mean either "in possession [of wisdom]" (fitting 8:18 and 9:4, 17) or "self-controlled/continent."
reason: Notes should explain the Greek, not report what another translation (the Vulgate) does; the lexical explanation is kept.

old: She rescued a devout people and blameless offspring from a nation of oppressors.
new: She rescued a devout people and a blameless seed from a nation of oppressors.
reason: σπέρμα ἄμεμπτον: OT convention renders σπέρμα as "seed" (as this book does in 3:16, 12:11, 14:6), not "offspring".

old: Following the Greek manuscript reading oneidos ('reproach') rather than the conjectural emendation orexin ('desire,' reflected in the Vulgate). The abrupt shift from plural 'the foolish' to the singular verb pothei ('one longs for') is a known syntactic difficulty in the Greek text.
new: Following the Greek reading oneidos ('reproach'); other witnesses read orexin ('desire'). The abrupt shift from plural 'the foolish' to the singular verb pothei ('one longs for') is a known syntactic difficulty in the Greek text.
reason: ὄρεξιν is a manuscript reading, not merely a conjectural emendation, and the remark on the Vulgate is a claim about another translation; state the variant neutrally.

old: This compressed philosophical sentence is notoriously difficult: 'expectation' (prosdokia) likely refers to expectation of aid from v. 11, and 'the cause' may be construed either as comparative ('greater than the cause') or as objective with 'ignorance' ('ignorance of the cause').
new: This compressed philosophical sentence is notoriously difficult: 'expectation' (prosdokia) likely refers to expectation of aid from v. 12, and 'the cause' may be construed either as comparative ('greater than the cause') or as objective with 'ignorance' ('ignorance of the cause').
reason: The "aids" (βοηθημάτων) are in v. 12 in this numbering, not v. 11.

old: And with like penalty a slave was punished together with a master, and a commoner suffered the same things as a king;
new: And with like penalty a servant was punished together with a master, and a commoner suffered the same things as a king;
reason: δοῦλος is rendered "servant" by this edition's OT convention (cf. 9:5 "Your servant"); this is the only "slave" in the book.

old: Since many great things have been given to us through the Law and the Prophets and the others who followed after them—for which Israel ought to be praised for instruction and wisdom, and since not only ought the readers themselves become knowledgeable, but lovers of learning should also be able to be useful to outsiders both in speaking and in writing—my grandfather Jesus, after devoting himself extensively to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books, and having acquired considerable proficiency in them, was himself also led to compose something pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that lovers of learning, becoming committed to these writings as well, might make much greater progress in living according to the Law. You are urged, therefore, to read with goodwill and attention, and to show forbearance wherever we may seem to fall short in some of the expressions we have labored over in translation; for things spoken in Hebrew do not have the same force in themselves as when they are carried over into another language. And not only these, but the Law itself, and the prophecies, and the rest of the books have no small difference when spoken in their original language. For when I arrived in Egypt in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes and stayed for a time, I found a copy of no small instruction; I therefore judged it most necessary myself to apply some diligence and labor to translating this book. Indeed, I have devoted much sleepless effort and skill over that span of time to bringing the book to completion and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to love learning, preparing their character to live according to the Law.
new: Since many great things have been given to us through the Law and the Prophets and the others who followed after them—for which Israel ought to be praised for instruction and wisdom, and since not only ought the readers themselves to become knowledgeable, but lovers of learning should also be able to be useful to outsiders both in speaking and in writing—my grandfather Jesus, after devoting himself extensively to the reading of the Law and the Prophets and the other ancestral books, and having acquired considerable proficiency in them, was himself also led to compose something pertaining to instruction and wisdom, so that lovers of learning, becoming committed to these writings as well, might make much greater progress in living according to the Law. You are urged, therefore, to read with goodwill and attention, and to show forbearance wherever we may seem to fall short in some of the expressions we have labored over in translation; for things spoken in Hebrew do not have the same force in themselves as when they are carried over into another language. And not only these, but the Law itself, and the prophecies, and the rest of the books have no small difference when spoken in their original language. For when I arrived in Egypt in the thirty-eighth year under King Euergetes and stayed for a time, I found a copy of no small instruction; I judged it most necessary myself to apply some diligence and labor to translating this book. Indeed, I have devoted much sleepless effort and skill over that span of time to bringing the book to completion and publishing it also for those living abroad who wish to love learning, preparing their character to live according to the Law.
reason: "ought ... become" lacks the infinitive marker ("ought ... to become"); and "therefore" has no basis in the asyndetic ἀναγκαιότατον ἐθέμην (the semicolon already carries the connection).

old: And with people she made her nest as an eternal foundation, and with their offspring she will be trusted.
new: And with people she made her nest as an eternal foundation, and with their seed she will be trusted.
reason: μετὰ τοῦ σπέρματος αὐτῶν: OT convention renders σπέρμα as "seed" (as Sirach does in 45:15, 45:21, 46:9), not "offspring".

old: Search her out and seek her, and she will be made known to you; and when you have taken hold of her, do not let her go.
new: Search out and seek, and she will be made known to you; and when you have taken hold of her, do not let her go.
reason: ἐξίχνευσον καὶ ζήτησον have no expressed object; the twice-supplied "her" is not in the Greek.

old: Be willing to listen to every godly discourse, and do not let proverbs of understanding escape you.
new: Be willing to listen to every divine discourse, and do not let proverbs of understanding escape you.
reason: θείαν is "divine" (of God), not "godly" (pious).

old: Do not seek authority from the Lord, nor a seat of honor from a king.
new: Do not seek leadership from the Lord, nor a seat of honor from a king.
reason: ἡγεμονία is rendered "leadership" in 10:1; "authority" is used for ἐξουσία (9:13; 10:4).

old: Do not exchange a friend for money, nor a true brother for the gold of Souphir.
new: Do not exchange a friend for a matter of indifference, nor a true brother for the gold of Souphir.
reason: This Greek reads ἀδιαφόρου ("an indifferent thing"); "money" follows the variant διαφόρου found in other editions.

old: "Money" renders Greek adiaphorou (literally "an indifferent thing"), an idiom used in Sirach for financial gain or price; "Souphir" is the Septuagint name corresponding to Hebrew Ophir, renowned for fine gold.
new: "A matter of indifference" renders adiaphorou (literally "an indifferent thing"); other witnesses read diaphorou ("money"). "Souphir" is the Septuagint name corresponding to Hebrew Ophir, renowned for fine gold.
reason: The note attributed to ἀδιάφορον the sense "money," which belongs to διάφορον (cf. 27:1); corrected to describe the reading accurately.

old: The terse Greek clause makron arrostema, skoptei iatros literally reads "a long illness, a physician mocks" (or "scoffs at"), differing from the Hebrew manuscript tradition, which speaks of a slight illness baffling the physician.
new: The terse Greek clause makron arrostema, skoptei iatros literally reads "a long illness, a physician mocks" (or "scoffs at").
reason: The claim that the Hebrew has the physician "baffled" is inaccurate (the Hebrew speaks of a slight illness at which the physician jests); removed the unreliable comparison.

old: What kind of offspring is honorable? Human offspring. What kind of offspring is honorable? Those who fear the Lord. What kind of offspring is dishonorable? Human offspring. What kind of offspring is dishonorable? Those who transgress commandments.
new: What kind of seed is honorable? Human seed. What kind of seed is honorable? Those who fear the Lord. What kind of seed is dishonorable? Human seed. What kind of seed is dishonorable? Those who transgress commandments.
reason: σπέρμα is rendered "seed" (literal collective singular) by this edition's OT convention, not "offspring".

old: Free people will serve a wise slave, and a man of knowledge will not grumble.
new: Free people will serve a wise household servant, and a man of knowledge will not grumble.
reason: οἰκέτης is "household servant" in this edition (7:20-21; 23:10); "slave" is reserved for δοῦλος.

old: Do not pretend to be wise in doing your work, and do not glorify yourself in the time of your distress.
new: Do not show yourself wise in doing your work, and do not glorify yourself in the time of your distress.
reason: μὴ σοφίζου is rendered "do not show yourself wise" in 7:5; "pretend" adds a nuance of insincerity not in the verb.

old: Many monarchs have sat on the ground, and the unsuspected one has worn a diadem.
new: Many monarchs have sat on the ground, but the unsuspected one has worn a diadem.
reason: ὁ δὲ ἀνυπονόητος: δέ marks the contrast between the fallen monarchs and the unexpected one.

old: The Greek clause "it has not corroded to the end" (ouk eis telos katiosen) implies that wiping a bronze mirror never removes its tendency to corrode permanently; the enemy's malice is never finished for good.
new: Greek ouk eis telos katiosen means "it has not rusted completely" (or "for good"), continuing the image of corroding bronze from v. 10.
reason: The note offered a confused interpretation not stated by the Greek; rewritten to explain the clause neutrally.

old: The Greek text reads 'in your gladness' (en euphrosyne sou), whereas the Hebrew text reads 'in your folly.'
new: The Greek text reads 'in your gladness' (en euphrosyne sou); some editions read 'in your folly' (en aphrosyne sou).
reason: The Hebrew does not read "in your folly" (it speaks of being like those lacking sense); the variant "folly" is a Greek reading (ἀφροσύνῃ).

old: The Greek text reads plural 'mouths' (stomasin) and 'a godly person' (eusebous), whereas the Hebrew and some witnesses read 'an ungodly person' (asebous).
new: The Greek text reads plural 'mouths' (stomasin) and 'a godly person' (eusebous), whereas other Greek witnesses read 'an ungodly person' (asebous).
reason: asebous is a Greek variant; the Hebrew has a different word ("the arrogant"), so attributing asebous to the Hebrew is inaccurate.

old: Remember that death will not delay, and the decree of Hades has not been shown to you.
new: Remember that death will not delay, and the covenant of Hades has not been shown to you.
reason: διαθήκη is "covenant" in this edition (11:20; 16:22; 17:12), and the literal sense is clear here.

old: Do not miss out on a good day, and may a portion of a good desire not pass you by.
new: Do not miss out on a good day, and do not let a portion of a good desire pass you by.
reason: μή σε παρελθάτω is a third-person imperative ("let it not pass"), not a wish.

old: All flesh grows old like a garment; for the decree from of old is, "You will surely die."
new: All flesh grows old like a garment; for the covenant from of old is, "You will surely die."
reason: ἡ διαθήκη is "covenant" in this edition (11:20; 16:22; 17:12); keep the same term as 14:12.

old: A thief is preferable to one who continually persists in lying, yet both will inherit destruction.
new: A thief is preferable to one who persists in lying, yet both will inherit destruction.
reason: ἐνδελεχίζων ψεύδει is "persisting in lying"; "continually" doubles the verb's sense with no separate Greek word.

old: A father's shame is in the birth of an undisciplined son, and a daughter is born to loss.
new: A father's shame is in the birth of an undisciplined child, and a daughter is born to loss.
reason: ἀπαιδεύτου (two-termination adjective) specifies no gender; "son" is supplied.

old: There is speech matched with death; may it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob. For all these things will depart from the godly, and they will not wallow in sins.
new: There is speech matched with death; let it not be found in the inheritance of Jacob. For all these things will depart from the godly, and they will not wallow in sins.
reason: μὴ εὑρεθήτω is a third-person imperative ("let it not be found"), not an optative wish.

old: Greek 'lampra kardia' ('a bright heart') denotes a cheerful or generous disposition, and 'epimelesetai' ('will attend to') conveys caring for or enjoying its food. From here through 36:16 the English keeps the Saints.Bible verse slots shared with the Latin edition (the restored chapter order); the Saints Greek Critical Text follows the manuscript order (Swete), so its verse numbers differ throughout this section.
new: Greek 'lampra kardia' ('a bright heart') denotes a cheerful or generous disposition, and 'epimelesetai' ('will attend to') conveys caring for or enjoying its food. From here through the end of chapter 36 the English keeps the Saints.Bible verse slots shared with the Latin edition (the restored chapter order); the Saints Greek Critical Text follows the manuscript order (Swete), so its verse numbers differ throughout this section.
reason: The parallel numbering extends to 36:26 (Greek 36:31).

old: This critical text does not include the line numbered 33:16 in some editions ('I was the last to keep watch'), so 33:17 opens directly with the participial comparison.
new: In this critical text the line numbered 33:16 in some editions ('And I was the last to keep watch') stands at the seam of the transposed sections and is rendered at 36:10, so 33:17 opens directly with the participial comparison.
reason: The note claims the critical text lacks the line, but it is present (Κἀγὼ ἔσχατος ἠγρύπνησα, printed in the input under Greek 36:16) and the English renders it at 36:10, whose note says so.

old: For in many foods there will be pain, and insatiability will draw near to colic.
new: For in many foods there will be pain, and insatiability will draw near to bilious nausea.
reason: χολέρα is rendered "bilious nausea" in 31:20 (where "colic" renders the different word στρόφος); using "colic" here gives one Greek term two renderings and two Greek terms one rendering.

old: Was not water made sweet by wood so that His power might be known?
new: Was not water made sweet by wood so that its power might be known?
reason: αὐτοῦ is ambiguous (nearest antecedent is the neuter ξύλου 'wood', or the Lord of v. 4); capitalized "His" silently decides it, so follow the nearest antecedent and note the alternative.

new: Or 'His power'; Greek autou may refer to the wood or to the Lord (v. 4).
reason: One-sentence note preserving the alternative referent of αὐτοῦ for the change above.

old: And in the assembly they will not rise to prominence, and they will not understand a covenant of judgment; they will not sit on a judge's seat, nor will they declare righteousness and judgment, and they will not be found among proverbs;
new: And in the assembly they will not rise to prominence, and they will not understand a covenant of judgment; they will not sit on a judge's seat, nor will they declare righteousness and judgment, and they will not be found among parables;
reason: παραβολαῖς is rendered "parables" in 39:2-3, where "proverbs" is reserved for παροιμιῶν; keep the same English here.

old: Many will praise his understanding; it will not be blotted out forever. His memorial will not depart, and his name will live for generations of generations.
new: Many will praise his understanding; forever it will not be blotted out. His memorial will not depart, and his name will live for generations of generations.
reason: ἕως τοῦ αἰῶνος οὐκ ἐξαλειφθήσεται means it will never be blotted out; "will not be blotted out forever" can be misread as 'not permanently' (wrong scope of negation).

old: the inheritance of the children of sinners will perish, and with their offspring reproach will remain continually.
new: the inheritance of the children of sinners will perish, and with their seed reproach will remain continually.
reason: σπέρματος is rendered "seed" (literal collective singular) per the edition's OT convention, as elsewhere in this section (45:15, 45:21, 46:9).

old: about the law of the Most High and the covenant, and about judgment to acquit the ungodly,
new: about the law of the Most High and the covenant, and about judgment to justify the ungodly,
reason: δικαιῶσαι is "to justify", the edition's rendering of δικαιόω throughout Sirach (7:5, 9:12, 13:22, 18:2, 23:11); "acquit" narrows the sense.

old: Greek dikaiosai ton asebe literally means 'to acquit the ungodly'; in context it either connects back to 'do not show partiality so as to sin' (42:1) or refers to judging impartially even when the verdict favors an ungodly person in a particular dispute.
new: Greek dikaiosai ton asebe ('to justify the ungodly') is legal language for declaring someone in the right; in context it either connects back to 'do not show partiality so as to sin' (42:1) or refers to judging impartially even when the verdict favors an ungodly person in a particular dispute.
reason: δικαιῶσαι literally means "to justify", not "to acquit"; note brought into line with the corrected verse.

old: With their offspring a good inheritance will endure, their descendants. In the covenants
new: With their seed a good inheritance will endure, their descendants. In the covenants
reason: σπέρματος is rendered "seed" per the edition's OT convention; "descendants" already renders ἔκγονα in the same verse.

old: their offspring stood firm, and their children because of them.
new: their seed stood firm, and their children because of them.
reason: σπέρμα is rendered "seed" per the edition's OT convention.

old: Forever their offspring will remain, and their glory will not be blotted out.
new: Forever their seed will remain, and their glory will not be blotted out.
reason: σπέρμα is rendered "seed" per the edition's OT convention.

old: Therefore by an oath He established for him that nations would be blessed in his offspring, to multiply him like the dust of the earth, and like the stars to exalt his offspring, and to cause them to inherit from sea to sea and from the river to the end of the earth.

old: But the Lord will never forsake His mercy, and nothing of His works will ever perish; nor will He ever blot out the descendants of His chosen one, and the seed of the one who loved Him He will never remove. And to Jacob He gave a remnant, and to David a root from himself.

old: The Greek text reads the proper name 'Gog' (τὸν Γώγ), widely understood as an ancient scribal corruption for the spring 'Gihon' (cf. 2 Chr 32:30), whose waters Hezekiah channeled into Jerusalem.

old: And may the bones of the twelve prophets sprout again from their place. Now He comforted Jacob and redeemed them in faithfulness of hope.

old: Woe, sinful nation, people full of sins, evil offspring, lawless sons! You have abandoned the Lord and provoked the Holy One of Israel to anger.

old: And the Lord Sabaoth became furious with anger against His people, and He laid His hand upon them and struck them; and the mountains were provoked, and their corpses became like dung in the middle of a road. And in all these things His fury has not turned away, but His hand is still high.

old: and there will no longer be a stronghold for Ephraim to take refuge, and no longer a kingdom in Damascus nor the remainder of the Syrians; for you are no better than the sons of Israel and their glory. Thus says the Lord of Sabaoth:

old: At that time gifts will be brought up to the Lord Sabaoth from an afflicted and plucked people, and from a great people from now and for eternal time, a nation that hopes and is trampled, which is in a part of a river of its country, to the place where the name of the Lord Sabaoth is, Mount Zion.

old: And the spirit of the Egyptians will be troubled within them, and I will scatter their counsel; and they will inquire of their gods and their images and those who call out from the ground and the ventriloquists.

old: And the earth acted lawlessly because of those who inhabit it, because they transgressed the law and changed the ordinances, an everlasting covenant.

old: The Septuagint reads "to Your beloved" (to agapeto sou) where the Masoretic Text has "before You, O LORD."

old: And again God will wait to have compassion on you, and because of this He will be exalted to have mercy on you, because the Lord your God is a judge; blessed are those who wait upon Him.

old: Lord, have mercy on us, for in You we have trusted; the offspring of the disobedient has come to destruction, but our salvation is in a time of distress.

old: Take courage, you who are fainthearted in mind; be strong, do not fear; look, our God renders judgment and will render it; He Himself will come and save us.

old: And this will be the sign for you: eat this year what you have sown, and in the second year what is left, and in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards and eat their fruit.

old: Now it happened at that time that Hezekiah became ill to the point of death; and Isaiah son of Amoz, the prophet, came to him and said to him, "This is what the Lord says: 'Give orders concerning your house, for you are dying and you will not live.'"

old: And now, have you not known? Have you not heard? An everlasting God, the God who constructed the ends of the earth, will not hunger nor grow weary, nor is there any finding out of His understanding,

old: In contrast to the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("the LORD loves him; he shall perform His purpose on Babylon, and His arm against the Chaldeans"), the Septuagint renders the clause in the first person addressed to Israel: "Loving you, I carried out your will against Babylon, to remove the seed of the Chaldeans."

new: Thus says the Lord: "If anyone takes a giant captive, he will take plunder; and one taking from a strong man will be saved; and I will judge your case, and I will rescue your sons;
